title: Study Abroad Experience at National Taiwan University
paragraphs: I was allowed to study at National Taiwan University for twelve weeks from March to June. Taiwan has deep ties with Japan, and National Taiwan University also has as its predecessor Taihoku Imperial University, which was established in the former colonial era. I had heard that medical education in English is thriving at National Taiwan University and that many students speak English fluently, and wanting to improve my own English in such an environment, I applied to study at National Taiwan University. In the clerkships, I studied for three weeks each in the Department of Radiology diagnostic imaging division, obstetrics and gynecology, the Department of Radiology nuclear medicine division, and anesthesiology.

In the diagnostic imaging division, starting from the early-morning journal club and conferences, I was allowed to attend lectures with local students, observe image acquisition, and observe catheter treatment. As for catheter treatment in particular, I was able to see cases rarely seen in Japan, such as cerebral angiography and catheter treatment for liver cancer.

In obstetrics and gynecology, I was allowed to attend lectures with local students, observe operations, assist with normal deliveries and cesarean sections, and visit obstetrics and gynecology clinics in the city. In Taiwan, chromosomal diagnosis of the fetus by amniocentesis is common and the state even provides subsidies, and I felt a difference from Japan. I was told that not only Taiwanese but also people who come all the way from Japan receive diagnoses there, and I could see how high the ability of National Taiwan University is in the field of obstetrics and gynecology.

In the nuclear medicine division, I gave presentations on the image diagnosis of my assigned cases and received lectures with local students. In the lectures, the method was that I first made slides on the content to be studied that day, explained using those slides myself, and then the teacher gave supplementary explanations. It is a way that one would almost never see in Japan, and I enjoyed doing it very much.

In anesthesiology, I was mainly allowed to observe the operating room. In Taiwan, one anesthesiologist apparently handles multiple operations at the same time, and I felt a difference from Japan. During the observation, I was allowed to observe thoracotomy, epidural anesthesia for cesarean section, and pediatric anesthesia, and I received a lecture on how to administer anesthesia. On the last day, at the morning conference I also gave a presentation on Japanese anesthesiologists and medical education.

Besides the clerkships, on holidays I walked around Taipei, traveled to the countryside, traveled abroad, and watched the inauguration ceremony of Taiwan's new president, and enjoyed the atmosphere of Taiwan and overseas to the full, but I also feel that three months was not enough. In and out of the clerkships, I sometimes felt the language barrier of Chinese, but at the same time I was helped by the kind consideration of the Taiwanese doctors, students and everyone in Taiwan, and was able to make it a very fulfilling study abroad.

Through this study abroad I was able to catch a glimpse of part of overseas medical settings and learn what overseas students think, and also learn how Japanese medicine is seen from overseas. I intend to work even harder so that I can make use of this experience, directly or indirectly, in my career as a doctor. Finally, I sincerely thank the professors of the International Collaboration Office, the people of the Academic Affairs staff, and everyone involved with the study abroad scholarship, who gave me such a wonderful opportunity. Thank you very much.
